## Build

### 2026-10-02 — # Ground Zero

**1h**

# Ground Zero

## Project Description

Ground Zero is a small battery-powered high-voltage prank device built around a compact high-voltage shock module. The goal was to experiment with high-voltage electronics, compact wiring, switching, insulation, and fitting everything into a small physical package.

The project started as a simple idea: take an inexpensive high-voltage module and turn it into a compact, portable device with a simple user interface and minimal components.

## Why I Built It

I wanted a project that I could actually finish quickly while still learning something about electronics. Instead of designing a complicated circuit from scratch, I focused on the physical implementation—how to package a high-voltage module, manage the wiring, make the device portable, and keep the high-voltage section isolated.

## Build

I assembled the battery supply, switch, high-voltage module, and output section into a compact setup. After completing the wiring, I tested the system and confirmed that the module was operating.

The main challenge was dealing with the high-voltage section. Even though the input power source is small, the module produces a much higher voltage, so insulation and keeping conductive parts isolated were important considerations.

## What I Learned

* How a small battery can power a high-voltage conversion module.
* The difference between the low-voltage input side and high-voltage output side.
* Why insulation becomes much more important when working with high voltage.
* How physical layout matters just as much as the electrical circuit.
* How to turn a simple module into a complete physical project.

## What Makes It Mine

The high-voltage module itself is an off-the-shelf component, but I designed the overall physical setup around it. I chose the power arrangement, switching, wiring layout, packaging, and overall form of the finished device.

The project is intentionally simple: the challenge was taking a basic module and turning it into a working, portable device rather than making the electronics unnecessarily complicated.

## Status

**Build complete.**

The wiring and setup are finished, and the device has been tested to confirm that the high-voltage module operates.

## Next Steps

If I continue developing it, I would improve the enclosure, make the wiring more organized, add clearer power/status indication, and improve insulation and physical separation around the high-voltage section.

## Parts

* Battery
* High-voltage/shock module
* Switch
* Connecting wires
* Insulation/heat-shrink
* Enclosure/material for mounting
* Miscellaneous mounting hardware

## Safety

This project contains a high-voltage circuit. The output is not intended to be connected to a person. Testing should be performed without using a person as part of the electrical circuit, with the high-voltage section insulated and handled carefully.

### 2026-10-02 — Circuit Design

**4h**

Circuit Design

I started by figuring out how the different parts of the circuit would connect. I used the high-voltage module as the main part of the circuit and planned the battery and switch connections around it.

I then started learning KiCad so I could draw the circuit as a proper schematic instead of keeping everything as a hand-drawn diagram.

While designing the schematic, I learned how to add components, connect wires, label connections, and organize the circuit. After checking the schematic, I used the design as a reference for assembling and testing the physical circuit.

This helped me understand how a circuit goes from an idea, to a schematic, and finally to a physical build.
